wingBreakStationSource: Lift-strut wing attach |y| 3.40 m (133.9 in) from the centreline: our own J-3 model (tools/own_models/build_j3_cub.py Y_ST, traced from the J-3 three-view). Checks: Piper spar drawing 14383 (J-3 to PA-18) puts the strut fitting 121.25 in from the root bolt hole, measured 123.5 front / 122.25 rear in from the spar root end on a PA-18 spar (supercub.org 'Spar Drilling', quoting drawings 14388/14453), plus ~13 in root-end offset (scaled) = 135-136.5 in; the PA-18 Information Manual three-view (p.4) scales to 129-131 in. 3.40 m sits inside that 130-136 in spread.
liftStrutFuselageAttachSource: Own J-3 model (build_j3_cub.py F_ST): one fitting for both V-struts on the lower longeron, 0.645 m (25.4 in) aft of the wing LE (the TCDS A-691 datum), BL 0.325 m (12.8 in), 1.16 m (45.7 in) below the wing chord line; put in this config's frame from its root wing LE (x 0.407) and chord line (z -0.75).

surfaces._airfoilNote: Ty 2026-11-10, told 26 of the 32 types fly their fin on a 2-D section: "All 26, own build". naca0012-like is 6.30/rad and NOTHING on this path applies a finite-span correction - a vStab never goes through FiniteSpanSection - so these fins carried about 69 % too much directional stiffness at small sideslip. fin-lowAR is 3.724/rad, no camber, zero Cm, Cl_max 1.16 held flat from 25 to 30 deg: a low-aspect-ratio plate, which is what a fin is, and what the rudder on this same tail already used. The hStab is deliberately NOT touched - that is the flat-plate fabric-tail question and it is separate.

crossflow.stationSource: Measured 2026-11-09 off the type's own three-view lines in tools/own_models/build_j3_cub.py (F_TOP, F_BOT, F_HW), the same tables the visual model is built from. The midline RISES 0.169 m by the fin station, which the constant-section crossflow body could not say at all (CentreZ was zero everywhere) - and an attached propeller wash needs a shape to follow. Owner 2026-11-09: the vortex has a tendency to follow the fuselage, not a rule, so PropJet traces attached and free and blends them.

spinAero.shadowKSource: Geometric helical shadow depth (TailWake.GeometricShadow): the share of dynamic pressure a fully shadowed strip loses. Replaces the Report 648 wake correlation for EVERY surface of this type, and brings in the fuselage's own shadow on the tail and the wings (TailWake.BodyStation). Ty 2026-11-08: "expand the shadow work to all 6 shipping aircraft include the shadow effects of the fuselage on the tail and wing's too". 0.5 is the depth fitted on the Pitts against the owner's spin attitudes on 2026-11-08, and it is a PHYSICAL statement - half the q is gone where a wake fully covers a section - rather than a per-type fudge, so the six carry the same number until a type's own evidence moves it. What differs between types is the geometry, which is the point: the Pitts' cellule shadows itself, the Extra's stabiliser spans well outside its fuselage and is barely shadowed at all (measured in a tumble: tail q 1.00 -> 0.96), and the fuselage's own shadow is what takes the fin in an upright flat spin while leaving it in clear air inverted.
spinAero.controlSpoilerKSource: A deflected control on a BROADSIDE surface acts as a spoiler on the separated wake, not as a flap: adds k*sin(delta)*|sin(alpha_chord)|*q*S normal to the FIXED surface's own plane, over hinged tail strips only, ramped in over 20 deg from controlSpoilerOnsetDeg. 0.6 is the PITTS' value and is carried unchanged, not refitted per type: it was fitted there on 2026-11-10 to Ty flying a clip of his own Pitts flat spin ("the elevator literally does nothing in the spin"), and pitts-s2b-like.json holds the sweep it came from - elevator authority at alpha 80 of 3.7 deg/s2 at k 0, 15.5 at 0.3, 27.4 at 0.6, 43.4 at 1.0, where 1.0 leaves the curve nearly flat from 30 to 90 deg and a plate should not be. WHY THIS TYPE HAS IT NOW. It shipped on the Pitts and the Extra alone, and that was STAGING rather than a finding: the argument for the term is about the SECTION - post-stall the section law is Cd_max*sin(theta), which is flat at broadside, so a strip model gives a control on a broadside surface a direction to point its force in and no magnitude to command - and when this type's horizontal tail became a flat plate on 2026-11-10 (b7396cd0: stall 9 deg, Cl_max 0.90, blend 44) that argument started applying to it too. Worse, the controlSpoilerOnsetDeg 10 that came with the plate was INERT here, because the spoiler block in AeroModel.Compute is gated on controlSpoilerK > 0.0: the onset was moving the start of a term multiplied by zero, and the hole it was meant to close was being closed by the 44 deg blend alone. Ty 2026-11-10, shown exactly that and the argument that the restriction to two types was staging: "Do it". MEASURED ON THIS TYPE (SpoilerFleetProbe, SPOILER_FLEET=1). Authority is the pitching moment the stick's whole travel commands at 30 m/s with the wind turned to the body alpha asked for, as a fraction of its own alpha 0 value; the floor is the worst of it over alpha 10-60 at a 0.5 deg step. Floor 0.117 at alpha 43 -> 0.225 at alpha 42; alpha 45 0.126 -> 0.237. IT COSTS THE PITCH DAMPING NOTHING, and for a mechanical reason rather than a lucky one: the term carries sin(gain*deflEff) and is gated on a non-zero deflection, so it cannot appear in a controls-neutral quantity, and dM/dq is one. VERIFIED rather than asserted, because if it had moved then the gate would not be what we think it is: the worst dM/dq over alpha 10-60 is BIT-IDENTICAL at k 0 and k 0.6 on all eleven configs that gained it and on the two that already had it. Vso AND THE TRIM ARE UNMOVED TOO, which was not obvious and had to be measured rather than argued: unlike stabHighAlphaK's 60-90 deg band, this term opens at 10 deg of the strip's OWN flow, and a tail strip with the stick near its aft stop at the stall is not self-evidently below that. It is - measured on the Stearman at its own Vso, the stabiliser's local angle is 2.74 deg against the 10 deg onset, because the downwash (3.49 deg there) and the stabiliser's own negative incidence take it out of the body alpha - so the ramp never opens in any ordinary flight condition and every type's Vso, trim alpha and trim elevator come out unchanged to the digit. WHAT IT DOES CHANGE is high-alpha pitch authority and therefore the spin, which is the point, and nothing below the ramp.
spinAero.controlSpoilerOnsetDegSource: The spoiler ramp starts at the SECTION'S OWN STALL. 30 deg was chosen when every hStab was a naca0012 (stall 14 deg); a flat plate stalls at 9-12, which left alpha 20-34 with no table effectiveness and no spoiler yet - and that band WAS the hole in the elevator authority. Worth the whole difference: authority floor 0.165 at onset 30 against 0.249 at onset 10. Ty 2026-11-10 accepted the plate knowing this moves the term he judged the Pitts' spin on.

propulsion.dryBoundaryExcessSource: Dry boundary friction excess at rest, over the power curve's own running friction intercept (PistonEngine.BoundaryFrictionFactor): 2.24 means this engine resists 3.24x its running friction when it is dead and dry. Continental C-85, 188 cu in, 4 cyl, CR 6.3, wood propeller. SOLVED 2026-11-10 (lane/claude-boundary-friction, CompressionStopProbe with COMPSTOP=1 SOLVE=1) against Ty's anchor "Cranking resistance should be calibrated such that at fine pitch the prop stops right at level flight stall speed", and then his "fix it per engine": it is the one value that puts the measured stopping speed on this type's OWN stall speed, 19.3 m/s = 43 mph (PracticeScenario.EstimateVso, sea level, flaps up - the number the rest of the suite is tuned against, not a book figure). Solved and not predicted: nothing inside an engine explains the fleet's spread, because motoring friction and rated torque both scale with displacement - see PistonEngine.BoundaryExcessFor for what was tried and rejected. THIS IS NOW THE ONLY THING IN THE DEAD-ENGINE MODEL THAT IS FITTED TO ANYTHING: the compression peak beside it is the engine's own gas load out of its displacement and compression ratio (PistonCompression.PeakNmFor), and the speed a stopped propeller breaks away at is a measurement rather than an anchor. Re-solving moves it about 0.1 because the sweep that measures the stopping speed steps 0.25 m/s. The fleet default for every type not yet solved is 3.0.
propulsion.bladePitchSource: Fitted 2026-11-09 to 2150 rpm static at full power, sea level — the owner's figure for his metal propeller, applied to both the wooden and the metal blade at his direction ("don't over think this just use 2150 static on both the wood and metal"). That pitch reaches the 2575 rpm redline at 84 mph at full throttle, which he confirmed. Static rpm for any fixed-pitch type with a TCDS is published there; take the middle of the range at sea level. Fit: PistonEngine.FitPitchForStaticRpm.
propulsion.propMaterialSource: Sensenich W72 laminated birch, the J-3 original
propulsion.propInertiaSource: Propeller + spinner + the crank's rotating parts, kg.m2. From the OWNER'S BLADE RULE (2026-11-09, tools/aircraft_builder/prop_inertia.py): each blade is 15 % of the net propeller weight with its centre of mass at 25 % of the DIAMETER from the axis, the rest being hub near the axis - because a heavy constant-speed hub contributes almost nothing to sum(m r^2), so a mass-weighted estimate overstates the couple. M 6.0 kg, D 1.83 m, 2 blades: blades 0.377 + hub 0.042 (k 0.10 m) + crank 0.05 = 0.47, against 2.4 before. MASS: ESTIMATED: a 72 in Sensenich W72 wood propeller is 13 lb; wood props of this size are 11-14 lb, far lighter than the 44 lb metal one. Continental A-65, four small cylinders. VALIDATION: the rule reproduces Hartzell's published two-blade polar moment to +18 % (1.412 against 1.198) and runs +60 % high on their three-blade one, so it is applied to two-blade types only.

gear.toeOutDegSource: Standard 2 degrees of toe-out on every taildragger's mains (Ty 2026-11-10: "Use 2 degrees toe out on all taildraggers standard unless I adjust based on feel"). A standing slip angle outboard on each wheel: level the pair cancel, and when one is loaded more its outboard side force is the larger, pushing the aeroplane back toward the light side - "The loaded tire tries to unload back to the other". The sign comes from each wheel's own y, so one value means outboard on both (LandingGear.ToeRad). Live-tunable in OPTIONS while flying.
gear.gearTypeSource: Rubber shock cord in the leather boots on the legs -- Ty 2026-11-10: "The cub bungees are in the black leather bags on the gear legs" (the model draws them: Shock_Boot_L/R). A bungee stores and gives back: "no rebound but plenty of travel", which is what the gear does -- its damper only ever sees the closing rate -- and why a Cub bounces.
gear.legPivotSource: Measured off the type's own model, which carries the real linkage rigged for animation (j3-cub-like-own.glb: Gear_Pivot_L at span 0.320, up -0.490, with Gear_HingeAxis_L 0.58 m aft on the same y -- the two lower-longeron pins the V legs hinge on, the Univair J-3 parts-list layout the model was built from). The drawn wheel touches at span 0.920, up -1.199, so the leg runs 0.600 m out and 0.709 m down from the pin: 1.18 m of track per side per metre of compression (LandingGear.SplayPerM). Ty 2026-11-10: "The cub has bungee too. Pivot at the fuselage attachment and so does the pitts."

gear.toeOutDegSource: The matching value for THIS wheel. Toe is per leg (LandingGear.ToeRad reads g.ToeOutDeg and takes the sign from the wheel's own y), so a value on one main and nothing on the other is not 2 degrees out on both -- it is 2 out on one wheel and dead straight on the other, a standing uncancelled side force of about 0.42 of that wheel's load (12 per rad x 2 deg) with nothing opposing it. The 2026-11-10 toe-out commit says "Sixteen types, both mains each" and wrote the field to the FIRST main only on fourteen of them; this is the other main on each, with the same number. Ty's knob (LandingGear.ToeOutOverrideDeg) always covered both, which is why the two types he was flying when he chose the number -- the Pitts and the Extra, the two the commit did write both -- felt right.

loading._cgLimitsSource: FAA TCDS A-691, J3C-65 (docs/WEIGHT-AND-BALANCE.md): datum = wing leading edge, body x +0.4073 (docs/pending/loading-arm-estimates.md: inner strip LE, anchor HIGH), so body x = 0.4073 - arm x 0.0254. C.G. range (+10.6) to (+22.7), one range at all weights: forward 0.13806 m, aft -0.16928 m. Gross: maxTakeoffMassKg 553.38 = 1220 lb.
loading._comment: seats[].eye is the seated pilot's EYE (owner Ty, approved 2026-10-31), body frame +x fwd, +y right, +z DOWN, measured on extended gear; the Cockpit camera sits exactly there. The PRIMARY seat is first. loading.seats[].station, loading.tanks[] and loading.baggage[] are the arms from docs/pending/loading-arm-estimates.md (Codex lane, 2026-11-01): a published TCDS/POH arm where the row is CONFIRMED, converted to this frame through that aircraft's anchor. maxKg is the published placard where the source gives one. referenceKg is UNCHANGED and still follows the 172's convention, so the reference loading reproduces the authored mass, CG and inertia exactly and nothing moves at spawn. Whether each airframe's authored massKg includes a pilot or fuel is still the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.
loading._legacyEmptyMassKgNote: the older weight-and-balance lane (e4755c9) authored emptyMassKg as a true EMPTY WEIGHT, excluding pilot and fuel. The current LoadingConfig reads that same key as 'what is left when every station is empty', and these types have no stations in the current schema, so every spawn loaded the aeroplane to its empty weight: the Great Lakes flew 258 kg light (816 -> 558), the Cub 206 kg (553 -> 347), the Swift 50 kg (330 -> 280). SessionSettings.ApplyLoadTo runs on EVERY spawn, so this was the flying mass in the game while the .NET tests, which do not call ApplyLoad, kept using the authored massKg. Set to 0 so it derives from mass.massKg again; the authored figure is kept below, unread, for the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.
loading._seatPlacardNote: maxKg is a CONVENTIONAL occupant placard (250 lb, and the J-3's own authored 300 lb), not a figure read from a POH. referenceKg follows the 172's convention: the primary seat carries the pilot that mass.massKg already includes, so the reference loading still reproduces the authored mass, CG and inertia exactly and nothing moves at spawn. Whether each airframe's authored massKg really includes a pilot is the open W&B decision in AGENT-LOG NEEDS YOU.

airspeed._unitsSource: Ty 2026-11-10 (era and category) and his earlier explicit call: 1938 fabric, and the J-3's own PERIOD panel has read mph since it was built (tools/own_models/build_j3_cub.py; InstrumentLibrary.PeriodVariants).
airspeed._unitsRule: Ty 2026-11-10, asked what rule the other 27 types follow after settling five by hand, chose "by era and category": "Vintage, fabric and experimental types read mph; anything certified modern or turbine reads knots." FlyingGame.Core.Instruments.AsiUnits carries the rule and the exceptions.
